scenes.heading: What pH measures
scenes.narration: Every water based solution contains hydrogen ions, and pH is simply the number we use to record how crowded with those hydrogen ions a particular solution really is.

scenes.heading: The zero to fourteen scale
scenes.narration: The familiar scale runs from 0 up to 14. Pure water sits exactly at 7, and chemists call that midpoint neutral because acid and base effects balance each other perfectly.

scenes.heading: The acidic side
scenes.narration: Readings below 7 mean the solution is acidic. Lemon juice sits near 2 and tastes sharp, while vinegar lands close to 3, which is why both of them work well in cooking.

scenes.heading: The basic side
scenes.narration: Readings above 7 mean the solution is basic, also called alkaline. Soapy water sits near 10 and feels slippery, while household bleach sits close to 13 and is far stronger.

scenes.heading: Putting it together
scenes.narration: So pH counts hydrogen ions on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral, anything lower counts as acidic, and anything higher counts as basic or alkaline instead.
